relations.note: Sarasvatī and her male counterpart Sarasvant are invoked in the same hymn.

relations.myth: Vow to protect the Golden Light scripture
relations.note: She appears before his assembly and vows to protect the scripture’s teachers, reciters, and hearers.

relations.myth: Protectors in the Golden Light Sūtra
relations.note: They appear alongside her as parallel royal and Dharma protectors without a discrete personal encounter.

relations.myth: Prosperity goddesses in the Golden Light Sūtra
relations.note: They appear separately in the scripture, and their prosperity functions later overlap without explicit identification.

relations.myth: Assimilation of the Harivaṃśa martial hymn
relations.note: Her chapter incorporates a hymn related to Durgā, producing textual assimilation rather than a narrated meeting.
One later Hindu genealogy presents Sarasvatī as Brahmā’s consort.
A conflicting later Hindu genealogy presents Sarasvatī as Brahmā’s daughter.
Another later tradition describes Sarasvatī as Brahmā’s emanated creative speech-power.

relations.note: She refuses or admonishes the violent dragon, causing him to repent and become a protector.
Developed local versions make the reformed dragon her consort, though other versions leave them apart.
After both reveal their divine identities, the dragon offers jewels while Benzaiten performs a celestial dance.
Amaterasu tells Shōmu that Benzaiten descended on Chikubushima and commands establishment of a sanctuary.
They were equated as female aquatic island deities, especially during Meiji shrine reclassification.
She became one of Enoshima Shrine’s official kami replacing or institutionally translating Benzaiten after separation.
